title: Puppy Nap and Sleep Schedule: What Is Normal and How to Plan Your Day
description: How much do puppies sleep? Learn what the sources say, a flexible nap and bedtime routine, signs your puppy may be overtired, and when to call the vet.
excerpt: What is normal puppy sleep, and how to plan naps and bedtime without a rigid clock.
seoTitle: Puppy Nap and Sleep Schedule: What Is Normal?

html:
Young puppies sleep a lot, often 18 to 20 hours a day according to the American Kennel Club. That sleep comes in many naps plus a longer stretch at night. No source we could verify gives a fixed number of hours for each week of age, so this guide focuses on a flexible pattern instead of a strict clock.

How to read this article

Facts with a source name come from the pages listed at the end. Anything marked (general guidance) is common trainer advice that we could not confirm in those sources. Use it as a starting point and watch your own puppy.

Why puppies sleep so much

Your puppy is growing and meeting a whole new world. VCA describes puppy energy as short bursts. At two months old, those bursts add up to only about four to six hours of the day. The rest is rest.

So a puppy who naps most of the day is usually normal. VCA also notes that most dogs, even adults, spend at least half of each day asleep, and that one puppy might sleep 10 hours a day while another sleeps 14. Both can be normal.

The basic rhythm

A simple loop works for most households (general guidance):

  1. Wake up and go outside for a potty trip.
  2. A short activity: a meal, play, a training game or sniffing.
  3. Back to a quiet spot to rest.
  4. Repeat.

AKC recommends potty breaks after waking, eating, drinking, playing and before bedtime. For daytime, PDSA suggests taking a puppy out every 2 to 3 hours. AKC says a puppy may nap about every hour or so, for 30 minutes up to two hours.

An illustrative day

This is an example only, not medical advice and not a prescribed routine. Puppies differ by breed, age, health and household. Move the times around and keep the order. Ask your vet if you are unsure about feeding times or bladder needs.

Time (example)What happens
7:00Wake, potty, breakfast, potty
7:45Short play
8:15Rest in a quiet spot
10:00Wake, potty, short training game
10:30Rest
12:30Wake, potty, lunch, potty
1:15Calm play, then rest
3:30Wake, potty, short outing or play
4:15Rest
6:00Wake, potty, dinner, potty
7:30Calm time, gentle chewing
9:30Potty, then bedtime
NightPotty break if your puppy wakes and needs one

Working full time? Our puppy schedule for working owners shows how to cover the middle of the day.

Set up a good resting spot

  • Quiet and dim. AKC suggests a quiet, dim sleep area.
  • A safe place. A crate, a dog bed or a quiet corner all work, according to AKC. PDSA suggests a bed or chill-out area that the family leaves alone.
  • Let sleeping puppies sleep. AKC says to leave a puppy alone when they are asleep.
  • Do not become the only way to fall asleep. AKC advises against a puppy depending on you to nod off.

New to crates? See our crate training guide.

Bedtime

Parts of this come directly from the sources, parts do not. We mark which:

  • A set bedtime and a calm wind-down (PDSA, AKC).
  • A potty trip right before bed (AKC).
  • Expect a night break for the first weeks (PDSA, AKC).
  • Dinner a few hours before bed (general guidance). AKC recommends limiting food for several hours before bedtime.
  • Water: do not take water away on your own. One AKC page mentions limiting water before bed, but AKC's potty training page does not restrict water, and we found no veterinary source that recommends it for puppies. Ask your vet before limiting water, especially for small breeds, hot weather or any health concern.
  • Where to sleep: Dogs Trust suggests avoiding shutting a puppy in a crate at night at first, and sleeping in the same room with a gradual move away. AKC lists a crate as an option for rest. Talk to your vet or trainer about what suits your puppy.

For crying and first nights, see puppy crying at night and your puppy's first night home. To fit potty trips around naps, see the potty training schedule.

Could your puppy be overtired?

AKC says too much stimulation and exhaustion can lead to unwanted behavior, but its page does not list specific signs. Trainers commonly describe an overtired puppy like this (general guidance, not from the sources below):

  • More biting or grabbing than usual
  • Sudden frantic running (see puppy zoomies)
  • Barking or whining with no clear reason
  • Not listening to cues they know
  • Hard to settle

These signs can have other causes, such as hunger, needing to go out or illness. If they show up, try a calm reset: potty, a quiet spot, something to chew. If your puppy seems unwell, call your vet.

Biting also has a training side, which we cover in how to stop puppy biting.

Troubleshooting

Won't nap. Check the basics (potty, hunger, temperature), then move to a quiet, dim spot (general guidance).

Only sleeps on you. AKC advises not letting a puppy become dependent on you to sleep. Try moving the rest spot gradually. A trainer can help.

Cries when put down. See the crying guide above. If your puppy stays distressed, Dogs Trust suggests asking your vet for a referral to an accredited behaviourist, since it can be separation anxiety.

Sleep suddenly changes. VCA says to contact your vet about excessive tiredness or lethargy, restless nights, appetite changes, potty changes, lack of interest in play or heavy snoring. Flat-faced breeds with snoring or gasping at night should see a vet.

When to ask a professional

  • Sudden changes in sleep, energy or appetite
  • Unusual tiredness, weakness or lethargy
  • Loud snoring or gasping, especially in flat-faced breeds
  • Ongoing distress when alone

This article is general information, not veterinary advice.

Want it written down?

quick: Young puppies often sleep 18 to 20 hours a day (AKC), in many naps plus a longer stretch at night. A repeating loop of potty, short activity and rest works better than a strict clock. Call your vet if sleep changes suddenly or your puppy seems unusually tired.

faq.q: How many hours should a puppy sleep?
faq.a: Young puppies often sleep 18 to 20 hours a day (AKC, PDSA). Needs vary, and VCA says 10 to 14 hours can also be normal for some puppies.

faq.q: How long should a puppy nap?
faq.a: AKC describes naps from about 30 minutes to two hours.

faq.q: Should I wake a sleeping puppy?
faq.a: AKC says to leave your puppy alone when they are sleeping. If you are worried about sleep, ask your vet.

faq.q: Does my puppy need a strict schedule?
faq.a: We did not find a source that requires one. A repeating pattern is easier to follow than exact times (general guidance).

faq.q: When will my puppy sleep through the night?
faq.a: We could not verify a reliable age, so we will not give one. Expect some night potty breaks in the first weeks (PDSA) and ask your vet.

faq.q: Can a crate be used for naps?
faq.a: AKC lists a crate, a bed or a quiet place. Introduce it gently and never use it as punishment.
